title: How a rainy afternoon in Montreal inspired an iconic Canadian board game

image.caption: Scott Abbott, left, Chris Haney and John Haney in 1982 on a boat docked beside the Old Boat Works, also known as Sheppard Boatworks, in Niagara-on-the-Lake, where the initial assembly and packaging of the first Trivial Pursuit games took place. (Submitted by John Haney)

blocks.text: The Sunday Magazine

The bestselling Canadian board game of all time has sold more than 100 million copies worldwide, in 17 different languages. On the game's 45th anniversary, co-creator John Haney offers a personal account of the game's creation in his new book, My Trivial Pursuits: The Inside Story of the Board Game That Conquered the World.
45 years later, what’s the secret behind Trivial Pursuit’s enduring appeal?
LISTEN | How Trivial Pursuit inspired generations to stay curious :
The Sunday Magazine18:54How this Canadian's questioning colour wheel inspired generations to stay curious
Scott Abbott says he remembers it like it was yesterday.
It was a rainy Saturday in Montreal, December 15, 1979. His roommate, Chris Haney, had just returned from grocery shopping with a Scrabble game in hand.
The two had been gearing up for a Scrabble showdown, but the game's $11 price tag sparked a conversation that would send them down a life-altering path.
“There must be a lot of money in games,” Abbott recalls Haney saying. “Why don’t we invent a game?”
Abbott threw out one word: trivia.

The idea wasn't entirely out of left field. Abbott, then a sports journalist with The Canadian Press, and Haney, a photo editor with the Montreal Gazette, often spent late nights at the Press Club firing trivia questions back and forth.
So Abbott grabbed a pencil and a scrap of paper, settled down at the kitchen table and started sketching.
And that was the birth of Trivial Pursuit a general-knowledge board game that became a global cultural phenomenon.
An archival image of 270 Landsdowne Ave. in Montreal where the idea for Trivial Pursuit was birthed on Dec. 15, 1979. (Submitted by John Haney)

The bestselling Canadian board game of all time has sold more than 100 million copies worldwide, in 17 different languages. The game also spawned television adaptations and made a fortune for its four creators — Abbott, Haney and his brother, John Haney, and their lawyer friend, Ed Werner. Early investors who put up just $1,000 saw their stakes grow to more than $1 million, Abbott says.

John Haney, now 80, offers a personal account of the game's creation in his new book, My Trivial Pursuits: The Inside Story of the Board Game That Conquered the World, released for the game's 45th anniversary.
“It’s legacy for me and for my children and grandchildren to actually know what happened,” Haney told Piya Chattopadhyay on The Sunday Magazine.
A game that spans generations
Abbot says he and the other founders were "flabbergasted" by the game's success.
“We were stunned at the beginning. We thought the game would appeal to our generation, baby boomers, and then we found out quickly that it appealed to everybody from eight-year-olds to 88-year-olds.”

Earl Holland Jr. of Salisbury, Maryland, remembers growing up playing Trivial Pursuit with his older sisters as a five-year-old child in a household that was obsessed with Wheel of Fortune and Jeopardy.

A self-described trivia enthusiast who “read encyclopedias” for fun, Holland Jr. remembers being drawn to the game’s “frantic pace” and “knowledge-building”. Decades later, that early fascination came full circle when he appeared as a contestant on the American television adaptation of the board game, hosted by LeVar Burton. His episode aired in late October.

Earl Holland Jr., far right, standing beside other contestants and host LeVar Burton, second from left, for the taping of an episode on the second season of The CW's Trivial Pursuit game show, on October 10, 2025. The episode aired on October 22, 2026. (submitted by Earl Holland Jr.)
For Holland, the secret ingredients behind Trivial Pursuit's enduring appeal are a combination of its ability to evolve with the times and bring people together — plus its impeccable timing.

“Its birth … it coincided pretty much around the era of the rebirth of quiz shows and Jeopardy and things like that,” said Holland. “It's a social activity. I think its ability to span decades and be flexible and versatile is something that is huge with different audiences, no matter how old you are.”
And if you ask the games’ creators, that was the whole point.
“A professor can play with a street sweeper. They compete together on the same level,” Haney said.
And that appeal may have been baked into the game from the very beginning.
From kitchen table to worldwide sensation

Michael Wurstlin was a 26-year-old freelance graphic designer when Haney and Abbott approached him in 1979 with a piece of cardboard covered in glued-on scraps of paper and a request to design their board game.
Wurstlin went on to create the iconic board artwork and scroll logo for the original Trivial Pursuit Genus edition, in exchange for five shares in the company.
But he wasn’t immediately convinced the project was destined for greatness.
“They were very scruffy guys, chain-smoking, I’m pretty sure they were drunk half the time,” Wurstlin said.
Still, he says he believes their irreverent, anti-establishment spirit was precisely what set the game apart.
One of the co-creators, John Haney, pictured with the original mockup for Trivial Pursuit, presented to graphic artist Michael Wurstlin in 1979. (submitted by John Haney)
Behind that laid-back attitude, however, was an almost obsessive commitment to getting the questions right.

“It became an all-consuming obsession,” said Abbott, recalling how they scoured everything from newspapers and magazines to television, movies and books for materials. “We couldn’t sit down for lunch without reading a ketchup bottle from top to bottom to see what questions might be on it.”
In a pre-Google world, verifying the answers to all 6,000 questions required onerous double-sourcing. Even then, Abbott says the first printing wasn’t without mistakes.
The first eight of thousands of questions John Haney wrote for the first edition of Trivial Pursuit. (submitted by John Haney)
A copy of a letter the Trivial Pursuit creators wrote to their shareholders asking for help selecting their "five favourite questions and answers." (Submitted by John Haney)
Getting the game into stores proved just as difficult.
After plenty of rejection, in 1981 a couple of stores in Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont., finally agreed to take a chance on the fledgling game.
There was nothing like seeing that game on a shelf. It was like a dream come true.John Haney, Co-creator of Trivial Pursuit
Demand quickly outpaced expectations. Before long, people were lining up around the block at Toronto's then-famous toy store, Mr. Gameways' Ark, to get their hands on a copy.
“We sold [close to] 1,200 games in basically less than two months before Christmas of ’81,” Abbott said. “By September 1982, we sold… 20,000.”

They got a Canadian distribution deal with Chieftain Products Inc., which held the Canadian rights to Scrabble at the time, and then an American distribution agreement with game manufacturer Selchow & Righter.
That deal helped propel Trivial Pursuit from a hometown hit into a global sensation.
By 1984, nearly 20 million games had been sold in the United States alone.
Former U.S. president Ronald Reagan and others play Trivial Pursuit aboard Air Force One in 1985. (Submitted by John Haney)
A 1988 TV Guide cover featuring all four of Trivial Pursuit's creators, promoting a TV movie based on their story, which was featured on CBC. (Submitted by John Haney)
Abbott recalls realizing just how famous they'd become during a 1985 press tour in Australia.

“We’re at the zoo in Melbourne, and we’re walking down a pathway, [some] 10 year old kids in front of us–they turn around and they say, ‘look, it’s the Trivial Pursuit guys!’ and they’re all clamoring and jumping all over us,” he said.

According to the Canadian Museum of History, Trivial Pursuit helped fuel a board-game boom throughout the 1980s and ’90s, inspiring Canadian inventors to chase similar success. Few came close, however.
Haney said the decision to sell to Hasbro in 2008 was simple.

"It had gotten too big and our baby had left the nest and taken on a life of its own." Haney says Hasbro kept the game going, bringing out new editions that he and his co-founders wouldn't have had the energy to do themselves.
"So we were very happy to sell it. We had a few beers that day.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Kayla McLean is a web journalist with CBC News in Toronto. She grew up in Brampton, Ont., and received her bachelor of arts in media production at Toronto Metropolitan University. Before joining CBC in 2024, she worked as a breaking news reporter at Global News Toronto — covering everything from crime, sports, festivals and politics.
